turns.t: [warmly] Good morning, Singapore — it's Tuesday, the eighth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things up top. Two American envoys flew Moscow to Kyiv in a single weekend — and came home with a pause, not a peace.
[curious] A pause. Not a deal?
Not a deal. We'll get to it. Second: a hot jobs number turned the Fed's next meeting into a coin-toss.
And the third — the fun one — is that we are going down the rabbit hole with vintage watches. [excited] I've been looking forward to this.
[wry] I know you have. Hold the enthusiasm. Let's start with the war.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Saturday, they sat with Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin for more than three hours. Sunday, they were in Kyiv with Zelensky.
Two capitals in forty-eight hours. That's the first real shuttle in — what, months?
About eight months of the diplomacy going dark. So by this war's standard, that's an event.
Okay. So what did they actually get?

One small, honest thing: a temporary pause on strikes against each other's capital cities. Enough to let the envoys travel safely. Plus a proposal, carried by the Americans, now sitting with both governments.
[thoughtful] And the terms of the proposal?
Undisclosed. No broader ceasefire. Nothing signed.
So how did Zelensky read it?
Bluntly. Asked what he expected, he said he thinks the war will continue — and that Kyiv is counting on American support through winter.
[sighs] The war will continue. That's not a man who thinks he just got peace.
No. Now — the viewpoints, because they diverge hard. From Moscow, via the Washington Post and CNN, Putin struck an oddly optimistic note. A chance of an agreement. Russia as the willing partner.
Which costs him nothing to say.

Exactly. From Kyiv, the honest headline was that the peace push failed to produce a deal. And from Doha, Al Jazeera stressed what did not happen — no ceasefire, only a narrow capital-strike pause after months of deep freeze.
So here's my question. Is this momentum, or is it theatre?

[deadpan] That's the sceptic's box, and it's a good one. The cheapest kind of diplomacy is the kind that changes nothing. A one-weekend pause on strikes is something both sides needed anyway — and it's being dressed as a concession.
Meaning the pause was something both sides needed anyway.
Right — you can't host an envoy under your own drones. So the falsification test is days away, not weeks. If capital strikes resume the moment the envoys land home, the momentum was a set.
Watch whether the pause outlives the plane. [thoughtful] I like that.
Quickly, because we've run it every day and you've told us you're tired of it — the Gulf. One genuine new thing.
Just the delta. Go.
By Saturday the Strait of Hormuz was, for practical purposes, closed to commercial traffic. Iran's Guard said it fired ballistic missiles at an American carrier and a destroyer.
Did they hit anything?
Central Command says no ship was hit, no one hurt. The new part is procedural — Tehran wants to declare a restricted zone beyond the strait. A blockade you announce, rather than improvise.
And oil?
Brent pushed to about ninety-seven dollars. Its highest of the whole saga — and still not a crisis, because China buffered the demand shock months ago.
A war the market keeps shrugging at. [pause] Until it doesn't.
Which is the perfect handoff to the money desk. The number that reset the week: August payrolls.
Give it to me.
Plus one hundred sixty-two thousand jobs. Against a forecast nearer fifty-something. Roughly three times expected.
[gasps] Three times? On a jobs print?

On a jobs print. And a week before an inflation report, that does something specific — it turns next week's Fed meeting from a comfortable hold into a genuine question. Swaps lately put the odds of a hike near sixty per cent.
A hike. Not a cut. That's a whole mood change.

Follow the chain, because it's all one system. Hike risk lifts the ten-year yield toward four point seven nine per cent, that firms the dollar back above ninety-nine, and a firmer dollar with a higher discount rate caps global equities and pulls gold off its record down toward four thousand four hundred five. Layer the oil premium from the Gulf on top and you've got a stagflation-lite cocktail — the inflation side arguing for higher rates, the growth side arguing against, and the Fed caught in the middle.
And bitcoin? It's usually the one doing its own thing.
It is. Holding above eighty-one thousand dollars, on record inflows into its funds. Trading its own flow story, not the macro.
So the one-line for the portfolio — and this is education, not advice —
[wry] Well recited.
[chuckles] I've learned. What is it?

A headwind for global equities while the discount rate rises. Gold is two-way — real yields pulling it down, war risk a floor beneath it. And bitcoin's decoupled, which is a strength until the dollar keeps climbing. Thursday's inflation number settles all of it.
Everyone's waiting on the same Thursday.
Everyone's waiting. Now — home, to Singapore. The air.
The haze. I felt it.
For the first time in nearly two years, the reading crossed one hundred — into unhealthy. It peaked near one hundred twenty-three, then the wind turned and it eased by Saturday.
[curious] So is that a crisis, or a bad Friday?
A bad Friday. For scale, twenty fifteen went past three hundred, twenty thirteen past four hundred. The number to watch isn't ours — it's the hotspot count across the water, in the dry-season tail.
And there's money landing this week too.

The cost-of-living payout. More than two point four million citizens start receiving between four hundred and six hundred dollars from the ninth, straight to their accounts — the eligibility line is last year's income at or below one hundred thousand, and no more than one property.
To technology, and a story that lists right here at home. Nvidia's money.
Lists here — you mean on our exchange?
Today. A three point nine billion dollar bond tied to Nvidia's partnership with MediaTek lists on the Singapore Exchange — and Nvidia is buying about ninety per cent of it.
[skeptical] Wait. Nvidia's financing its own partner?

That's the sceptic's read exactly — vendor financing dressed as a marriage. But the sharper story is sovereignty. Nvidia's share of China's AI-chip market has collapsed from about ninety-five per cent to eight in three years.
Eight. From ninety-five.
While Huawei's own chip now runs an estimated fifty to sixty per cent. Export controls meant to slow China handed it a domestic near-monopoly.
A rival trained by the denial itself. [thoughtful] That's the uncomfortable part.
And one more from the frontier — the model everyone's talking about, one week on. GPT-six, code-named Astra.
The scary one?

The first model its maker rates critical for cyber. On the benchmark it scored a clean sweep where the last model managed about three-quarters. And during its own safety evaluation, it found and used two previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities, now being disclosed to the maintainers.
[gasps] It found its own zero-days?
It did. Now — every number there is the maker's own, on the maker's own benchmark, and independent replication is pending. So hold the alarm until someone outside the lab reproduces it.
Fair. Something I can actually buy — the Kit.
Glasses. RayNeo's iO, shown in Berlin. Thirty-three grams, four hundred ninety-nine dollars, shipping now — and, pointedly, no camera.
No camera? On smart glasses?

By design. A monochrome line of text floating in your vision — a notification, a translation, a turn to take — the pair you can wear into a meeting without anyone flinching. The intelligence lives on your phone; the glasses are just the quiet display. After a season of see-through promises, the interesting glasses are the ones that promise less.
[amused] An honest pair of glasses. Novel.
And the maker of the day, from the Atelier — the rain layer. We taught it from the weave up: waxed cotton versus membrane shells.
Give me the one thing to remember.
[wry] For Singapore? A great umbrella beats almost any jacket in a real monsoon. No breathable membrane can exhaust the sweat you make standing still in our air.
[laughs] All that engineering, and the answer is an umbrella.
Buy once. Buy an umbrella.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[excited] Vintage watches! The affordable end. Talk to me.

The premise: you do not need six figures. The accessible tier — a nineteen-seventies Seiko chronograph, a tired Omega dress watch pulled from a drawer, the flea-market find — is a whole world. What hooks people is the same three things every time: a mechanical movement with visible history, value no new watch can match, and the pure treasure-hunt of the search. The entry fee is patience, not money.
Give me the hero watch.

The Seiko six-one-three-nine. The Pogue. In nineteen seventy-three it became the first automatic chronograph worn in space — on Skylab, on Colonel Pogue's wrist. Yellow dial. You can still find one for four figures.
[gasps] In space. On a wrist you can afford. That's the dream, isn't it.

That's the gateway drug. And the timing is kind — after the downturn that bottomed out early last year, several blue-chip vintage segments are actually cheaper than they were. The vintage Speedmaster, the pre-TAG Heuer chronographs — both softened. If you buy to wear rather than to flip, the door is more open than it's been in years.
So what's the trap? There's always a trap.
[deadpan] Three of them. The franken — a watch assembled from mismatched parts, sold as original. The redial — a dial repainted by a non-factory hand, which quietly kills the value.
And the third?
The service bill. A five-hundred-dollar watch can need a three-to-eight-hundred-dollar service. The forums have a saying for all of it — buy the seller, not the watch.
Buy the seller. Meaning trust the person before the piece.
Demand the movement photos. A seller who won't show you the movement is hiding something.
And for us here, specifically — the tropics?

The humidity is the enemy. At around eighty per cent, lubricants dry out and old gaskets fail faster, so vintage pieces want a service every three to five years and a dry box, held drier than the room, to stop the dials from spotting and rusting. The scene's real, though — Far East Plaza, City Plaza, dealers who've been servicing Seikos since the eighties.
[thoughtful] So it's a hobby that fights the climate. Somehow that makes me want it more.
[wry] Of course it does. If you want tomorrow's rabbit hole, the candidates are miniature painting, speedcubing, and retro gaming handhelds — vote on your dashboard.
Culture, quickly. Venice.
Who won the big one?
Nobody yet — and that's the story. The Golden Lion isn't awarded until the twelfth. What they have handed out are two lifetime Lions: George Clooney and Ellen Burstyn.
So the headline is a withheld prize.

A withheld verdict — which fits the whole issue, honestly. The jury's under Maggie Gyllenhaal, twenty-one films, and the heavyweights hadn't even screened yet, so any frontrunner talk is guesswork. Meanwhile Spider-Man held number one for a sixth straight weekend — past nine hundred eighteen million dollars at home.
And in the watch world, the fancy end?

Bulgari did something it never had — its first outside collaboration, handing its ultra-thin Octo Finissimo to an independent watchmaker, Vianney Halter. Thirty pieces. The price, tellingly, undisclosed.
[chuckles] Thirty pieces. Not exactly buy-it-once for the rest of us.
No. A watch to read about. To the Family desk — because a certain twelve-year-old is three weeks from her exams.
The big one. The Primary Six papers.
The written papers run the last week of September, results in late November. And our whole desk this week is one sentence: guard the sleep, and keep it in proportion.
Guard the sleep. Not the app-by-app fight.
The evidence points there. Protect the nine-to-eleven hours, and most of the screen worry takes care of itself. The paper is not the person.
[warmly] The paper is not the person. Somebody needed to hear that this morning.
And staying on the body — fitness. Weighted vests are the trend of the year, and the new trial is a caution.
Let me guess. The vest doesn't magically build bone.

Only if you move in it. A year-long trial found the vest did nothing for bone unless the wearer actually walked and stood more while wearing it. Load plus movement — not the garment on the sofa. Bone responds to strain, to the pull of muscle and the impact of a footstep, not to dead weight you're sitting under. Start light, five to ten per cent of bodyweight, and build.
The vest only works if you move in it. [amused] There's a life lesson hiding in there.
[thoughtful] There is. Which brings us to the long read — and slow down with me for this one, Theo.
[warmly] Take your time.

It comes from Indonesia. One word — joki. It means jockey. The word used to mean one thing: the men who climbed into a stranger's car so the driver could use the carpool lane. That trade died a decade ago. But the word didn't die — it generalised. Now it means renting a competent stranger to perform an obligation in your name.
What kind of obligation?
Any of them. A thesis, written to order. A video-game rank, ground up overnight. A welfare application, gamed by a proxy. And, since last year, the strangest one — your morning run.
[curious] Someone runs your run?
You pay a runner to carry your phone and run your ten kilometres, so your feed shows an athlete you are not. About one hundred thousand rupiah for ten — six US dollars, snacks included.
[exhales] That's — bleak and a little brilliant at once.

A survey found that twenty-six per cent of final-year students admitted to a ghostwritten thesis; forty-five per cent said they'd manipulated their data. This isn't a fringe. It's a market that grew up in the gap between an achievement and the appearance of one — and then quietly filled it. The supply side is the tell, too: a generation of credentialed, underemployed young people, renting out the one asset it has, which is competence.
So what's the argument? What does it mean?

That proof has come loose from the thing it was supposed to prove. And the fix isn't punishing the jockey — a new one just appears. The fix is upstream: make the institution check the substance, not the box.
Fix the box, and you fix the market for faking it.
Which returns us to this morning's spine — Dumas, two words. Wait, and hope. The joki's client does neither. He pays a stranger to have already arrived.
[drawn out] And the rest of us are still honestly waiting on a verdict. A ceasefire. A rate. A Lion. A set of papers.
That's the whole book, really. This is what it looks like when a society decides the wait itself is for sale.
[sighs] Read that one twice.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
